query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A Ti–Ni primary HEA with a minor 5 at.% aluminum addition, when subjected to an aging treatment at approximately 800 °C for 1 hour, will form a high volume fraction (~20–30%) of coherent γ′ (L12) nanoprecipitates, resulting in enhanced elevated-temperature yield strength by ~20–30% relative to the same alloy processed in the as-cast condition.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline Ti–Ni primary high-entropy alloy (e.g., with principal elements Ti and Ni at ~30 at% each and three other elements (e.g., Co, Cr, Fe) distributing the remainder equitably within 5–35 at% limits) in as-cast, single-phase solid-solution form.
generation.intervention: Introduce 5 at.% aluminum (by partially replacing one or more minor elements) and perform an aging heat treatment at 800 °C for 1 hour.
generation.conditions: Aging heat treatment at 800 °C for 1 hour in an inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation; overall alloy composition remains within the 5–35 at% constraint per element.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent, nanoparticulate γ′ (L12) precipitates (e.g., of stoichiometry close to (Ni,Ti)3Al) uniformly distributed within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening: the coherent γ′ precipitates impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures, thereby increasing yield strength and creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement in yield strength at ~800 °C by approximately 20–30% compared to the baseline single-phase alloy, with additional benefits in coarsening resistance under sustained high-temperature operation.
generation.baseline: The same Ti–Ni primary HEA without the Al addition and without the aging treatment (i.e., as-cast single-phase alloy).
generation.boundary: Valid for elevated temperatures around 700–800 °C and for compositions that respect the high-entropy criterion (5–35 at% each); limited by the solubility and phase stability ranges of the constituent elements.
generation.uncertainty: Exact precipitate volume fraction, long-term coarsening behavior, and potential influence on ductility; potential sensitivity to minor compositional fluctuations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) the baseline Ti–Ni primary HEA without Al addition and aging, and (b) the modified alloy with 5 at.% Al followed by aging at 800 °C for 1 hour. Characterize both sets via TEM to quantify γ′ precipitate volume fraction and via high-temperature mechanical testing (tensile or compression tests) at ~800 °C.
measurements: TEM imaging and diffraction analysis to verify precipitate formation and coherence.
Creep rate measurements under constant load.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged, Al-containing alloy does not exhibit at least a 20% increase in elevated-temperature yield strength and corresponding evidence of coherent γ′ precipitates relative to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of elements with similar metallic atomic radii but different crystallographic structures (Al and Ti) to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy caused higher solution strengthening by the element with a different crystallographic structure than the solvent. The solid solution strengthening coming from addition of 5 at. pct Al to the Co-Ni-Fe alloy is negligible, while the addition of 5 at. pct of Ti significantly increases the solid solution strengthening. The precipitation hardening effect related to the presence of (CoNi)3Ti phase caused by the addition of 5 at. pct Ti is comparable with the total effect of the 5 at. pct Al and 5 at. pct Ti addition, which caused the precipitation of γ′ ((NiCo)3AlTi). Precipitation hardening is much greater in the investigated alloys than the solid solution hardening. We showed a successful way for effectively strengthening the FCC-HEA system (NiCoFe) using a small Ti addition. The microstructure obtained in the M3 alloy consists of precipitates with an L12 structure and structurally coherent with FCC matrix. We showed one of the ways of searching for new high-entropy alloys.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn significant attention due to their unique design and superior mechanical properties. Comprising 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, HEAs exhibit high configurational entropy, resulting in single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly direct energy deposition (DED), is effective for producing HEAs due to its rapid cooling rates, which ensure uniform microstructures and minimize defects. These alloys typically form face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, contributing to their exceptional strength, hardness, and mechanical performance across various temperatures. However, FCC-structured HEAs often have low yield strengths, posing a challenge for structural applications. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was manufactured using the DED method. This study proposes that the addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, enhancing the thermal stability and coarsening the resistance and strength. First, our selected strengthening phases are ductile, highly coherent and low misfit with matrix (i.e. they can compatibly deform with the matrix), implying that increasing their content does not significantly degenerate the ductility. Controllable microstructure (by either alloying or processing design) provides numerous possibilities for the optimization of properties; for instance, the strength of our alloy can be controlled within a very wide range, at least, of ~270–1900 MPa, and the largest elongation is >40%. Furthermore, benefiting from the advantages of the multi-principal-element/high-entropy matrix, high Cr addition can improve the resistance to corrosion and oxidation, and high Al content reduces the alloy density. These advantages present the potential for the application of our HEA to many rigorous service conditions, such as those subjected to very large loading and involving highly corrosive environment. papers.title: Manufacturing of Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti High-Entropy Alloy Using Directed Energy Deposition and Evaluation of Its Microstructure, Tensile Strength, and Mic
papers.system: Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti high-entropy alloy with a γ (FCC solid solution) plus γ′ (ordered L12) phase structure
papers.approach: Add Al and Ti to form a two‐phase microstructure (γ + γ′) via DED processing with controlled composition, targeting an ordered precipitate phase.
papers.findings: Alloys with an optimized Al+Ti content developed a γ + γ′ microstructure, where the γ′ phase (with near stoichiometric (Ni,Co)3(Ti,Al)) enhanced thermal stability, coarsening resistance and maintained strength (e.g., at ~800°C).
papers.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening via formation of coherent, ordered γ′ precipitates that impede dislocation motion at elevated temperatures.

papers.title: The Effect of Al and Ti Additions on Solid Solution Strengthening and Precipitation Hardening in CoNiFe Medium-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Co-Ni-Fe based medium-entropy alloys with additions of Al and Ti
papers.approach: Addition of 5 at.% Ti (and/or small Al) to promote precipitation of (CoNi)3Ti and/or γ′ ((NiCo)3AlTi) phases to overcome the low yield strength of single-phase FCC HEAs.
papers.findings: A minor Ti addition produced significant precipitation hardening that outweighed the negligible effect from Al addition alone, leading to considerably higher overall strengthening.
papers.mechanism: Precipitation hardening by forming coherent nanoprecipitates which act as barriers for dislocation motion.

papers.title: Influence of Titanium on Microstructure, Phase Formation and Wear Behaviour of AlCoCrFeNiTix High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNiTix high-entropy alloys with varying Ti content
papers.approach: Systematic variation of Ti content to study its effect on phase formation and mechanical properties
papers.findings: Increasing Ti content transformed the microstructure from a single phase to multiphase (including ordered and disordered BCC phases and, at high Ti contents, even fcc and complex phases) with enhanced hardness and wear resistance.
papers.mechanism: Titanium’s large atomic radius induces lattice distortions and promotes the formation of secondary (precipitate) phases that contribute to strengthening.

papers.title: High-content ductile coherent nanoprecipitates achieve ultrastrong high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: Non-equiatomic HEAs with a near-equiatomic FCC matrix and high-content L12 nanoprecipitates
papers.approach: Utilization of spinodal decomposition and control of Ni/Al ratio to produce high quantities of ductile, coherent Ni3Al-type nanoprecipitates
papers.findings: The designed HEA achieved an ultrahigh tensile strength (~1.9 GPa increase >560%) while retaining good ductility (>9%), attributed to the high volume fraction, coherence, and ductility of the L12 precipitates.
papers.mechanism: A spinodal order–disorder nanostructure that produces a coherent precipitate network, effectively blocking dislocation glide and imparting both high strength and ductility.

established: Precipitation strengthening via formation of coherent precipitates (e.g., γ′ or L12 phases) improves high-temperature yield strength in HEA systems.
Solid solution strengthening, while contributory, is less effective than precipitation hardening at elevated temperatures.
Careful balance of alloying elements (with similar atomic radii) allows retention of high configurational entropy and single-phase or controlled multiphase microstructures.

approaches_tried.approach: Addition of Al and Ti in Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEAs to achieve a dual-phase (γ + γ′) structure
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced thermal stability and strength retention at around 800°C, alongside improved coarsening resistance.

approaches_tried.approach: Minor Ti (and Al) additions in Co-Ni-Fe based alloys to induce precipitation hardening via Ni3Ti-type phases
approaches_tried.outcome: Substantial precipitation strengthening observed, significantly improving yield strength compared to mere solid solution effects.

approaches_tried.approach: Variation of Ti content in AlCoCrFeNiTix HEAs to modify phase composition and microstructural heterogeneity
approaches_tried.outcome: Increased Ti leads to multiphase structures, higher hardness and improved wear behavior, though excessive Ti can result in detrimental intermetallics.

disagreements: The relative contributions of solid solution strengthening versus precipitation hardening in improving high-temperature performance, particularly in complex HEAs.

open_questions: How does the high-volume, primary incorporation of both Ti and Ni (as opposed to their role as minor additions) affect the kinetics and thermodynamics of precipitate formation at elevated temperatures?
What is the optimal minor alloying addition (e.g., Al) and heat treatment protocol to stabilize a coherent precipitate phase in a Ti- and Ni-primary high-entropy alloy?
How do changes in composition influence creep resistance and long-term mechanical stability at elevated temperatures?
opportunities: Investigate the effect of introducing a controlled, minor addition (such as 3–7 at.% Al) into a Ti- and Ni-primary HEA to stimulate in situ formation of coherent γ′ (L12) precipitates.
Explore heat treatment and thermomechanical processing protocols tailored for Ti-Ni primary compositions to optimize precipitate size, distribution, and coherence at temperatures of 700–800°C.

Study the interplay of primary elements (Ti and Ni) with a minor element addition in the high-entropy compositional space (elements within 5–35 at% each) to determine improved yield strength and creep resistance relative to untreated alloys.

directions.direction: Introduce a minor addition of aluminum along with an aging heat treatment to promote the formation of coherent γ′ (L12) precipitates in the Ti‐ and Ni‐primary HEA.
directions.assessment: Directly targets elevated-temperature strengthening by inducing precipitation hardening without upsetting the high-entropy compositional balance. Physics and prior reports on γ+γ′ microstructures support its feasibility. It uses well‐established processing parameters and known mechanisms from HEA and superalloy literature.

directions.direction: Incorporate a small volume fraction of Y2O3 via powder metallurgy processing to achieve in situ nano-oxide dispersion strengthening in the Ti-Ni primary HEA.
directions.assessment: Acts directly on elevated-temperature yield strength and creep resistance by impeding dislocation movement. Supporting evidence from oxide‐dispersion strengthened HEAs suggests feasibility, though integration in a Ti–Ni primary system is less explored and may face processing challenges.

directions.direction: Add a minor amount of molybdenum (Mo) with a subsequent aging treatment to induce an ordered, possibly B2, two‐phase microstructure within the Ti‐Ni primary HEA.
directions.assessment: Mo is known to contribute to solid solution and precipitation strengthening in HEAs. The intervention could stabilize high-temperature phases and promote the formation of coherent precipitate interfaces. The physics is supported by literature on Mo-containing refractory HEAs, though phase stability boundaries must be carefully controlled.

directions.direction: Employ a tailored thermomechanical processing route (e.g., hot rolling followed by cold rolling and a short annealing treatment) to refine the grain structure and produce a bimodal microstructure in the Ti–Ni primary HEA.
directions.type: Processing or thermomechanical treatment and microstructure control
directions.assessment: Grain refinement and a controlled heterogeneous structure can improve yield strength at elevated temperature and enhance creep resistance. Although grain-boundary relaxation at high temperature is a concern, optimizing processing parameters to achieve a stable, bimodal distribution is feasible and supported by previous work in medium- and high-entropy alloys.

candidates.hypothesis: A Ti–Ni primary HEA incorporating 3 vol.% Y2O3 via powder metallurgy will in situ form a uniform dispersion of nanometer-scale Y2O3 particles during spark plasma sintering, thereby increasing the elevated-temperature yield strength by ~15–25% compared to the same alloy processed without the oxide addition.
candidates.intervention: Incorporate 3 vol.% Y2O3 nanoparticle precursor into the alloy powder prior to spark plasma sintering.

candidates.hypothesis: A Ti–Ni primary HEA with a 5 at.% Mo addition, followed by an aging treatment at 850 °C for 1 hour, will develop a two-phase microstructure comprising a B2-ordered matrix with finely dispersed Mo-rich ordered precipitates, leading to an improvement in elevated-temperature yield strength by approximately 20–30% compared to an alloy without the Mo addition and aging.
candidates.intervention: Modify the alloy by substituting 5 at.% of one of the minor elements with Mo and apply an aging heat treatment at 850 °C for 1 hour.

candidates.hypothesis: A Ti–Ni primary HEA subjected to a combined thermomechanical processing route—initial hot rolling (50% reduction) followed by cold rolling (70% reduction) and a short annealing treatment at 1100 °C for 10 minutes—will develop a bimodal grain structure that results in an elevated-temperature yield strength improvement of around 15–25% compared to the conventionally cast alloy.
candidates.intervention: Apply a processing route consisting of hot rolling (approximately 50% thickness reduction), then cold rolling (approximately 70% reduction), followed by a brief annealing at 1100 °C for 10 minutes to induce partial recrystallization and grain structure refinement.

minor_issues: Short annealing time (10 minutes) may not fully stabilize the bimodal grain structure across all regions of the alloy.

fixes: Extend or vary annealing durations to confirm stable bimodal microstructures and identify optimal processing conditions.
Examine different rolling schedules and orientations post-processing to understand and mitigate texture effects.
